modified_duration.text: `yield_to_call` answers "what yield would I earn if the bond is redeemed at its first call date?" It takes an observed dirty `price`, the coupon terms, a `call_price` and a `call_date` in years, then solves for the yield on the cashflows up to that date. `modified_duration` answers a different question: "how sensitive is the price to a change in yield?" It takes cashflows, times and a `yield_rate` you already have, and gives Macaulay duration divided by (1 + y/m), which approximates the percentage price change for a 1-unit yield move. So `yield_to_call` produces a yield from a price, while `modified_duration` starts from a yield and describes price sensitivity. You could use the yield from one as an input to the other, though they measure different things.

explain.text: `yield_to_call` (Yield To Call) gives the yield on a bond assuming it is redeemed at its first call date instead of running to maturity. It builds the coupon cashflows only up to `call_date` (time to the call in years), adds redemption at `call_price`, and solves for the yield that makes the discounted cashflows equal the observed dirty `price`. Coupons are sized from `face_value` and `coupon_rate`, paid `frequency` times a year (default 2). The number of periods is `call_date` times `frequency`, rounded.

when.text:
`yield_to_call` (Yield To Call) fits when you want the yield on a bond assuming it is redeemed at its first call date instead of running to maturity.

- You have an observed dirty `price` and want the yield if the issuer redeems at `call_price` at `call_date`, given in years.
- The bond is callable and you want to see the return under the early-redemption case, not just the hold-to-maturity case.
- You know the coupon terms: `face_value`, `coupon_rate` and `frequency` (payments per year, default 2).
- You want the cashflow stream cut off at the call date, with redemption at the call price in place of par.
- For a flat-rate yield assuming the bond runs to its final date, use `yield_to_maturity`, which pyvar lists as the flat rate that discounts cashflows to `price`.
